A.explanation: The power falls from about $3.27\text{ W}$ to about $0.86\text{ W}$, a decrease of about $2.4\text{ W}$.

B.explanation: This is close to the initial power in X alone, not the difference between the $0\,\Omega$ and $40\,\Omega$ cases.

C.explanation: This results from an error in total resistance, for example omitting the $2.0\,\Omega$ internal resistance when finding current.

D.explanation: This is too large and does not match $P=I^2R$ with $I=E/R_{total}$ for both settings.

hints: Notice the $12\text{ V}$, $2.0\,\Omega$, $40\,\Omega$ resistor X and $0-40\,\Omega$ variable resistor are all in one series loop.
Recall that series current is $I=E/(r+R_X+R_{var})$ and power in X is $P=I^2 R_X$ with $R_X=40\,\Omega$.
Calculate $P$ for $R_{var}=0\,\Omega$ and for $R_{var}=40\,\Omega$, then subtract to find the fall in power.
walkthrough: Identify the series total resistance for each setting. With internal resistance $2.0\,\Omega$ and $R_X=40\,\Omega$, $R_{total}=2.0+40+R_{var}$.
Power in X is $P=I^2R_X$. So $P_1=(2/7)^2 \times 40=160/49 \approx 3.27\text{ W}$.
Then $P_2=(6/41)^2 \times 40=1440/1681 \approx 0.86\text{ W}$. Increasing series resistance lowers current and so lowers $I^2R$ in X.
Change in power is $P_1-P_2 \approx 3.27-0.86 \approx 2.4\text{ W}$. This is option A.
